sections.html: Savannah is the oldest city in Georgia and the Chatham County seat, and its low ground and historic core affect how houses change hands. The 2020 census counted 147,780 residents, with an estimate of 149,440 for 2025. The city sits on the Savannah River about 20 miles upriver from the Atlantic, and a steady base of renters, students and workers means a house you are selling may also appeal to a buyer who plans to rent it out.

sections.h2: Which neighborhoods and historic districts affect a sale?
sections.html:
More than 100 neighborhoods fall into six principal areas, and the label on your street changes what buyers expect.

  • Downtown: the Landmark Historic District and the Victorian District, built around the Oglethorpe Plan and its 22 squares.
  • Midtown: the central area between downtown and the Southside.
  • Southside: the southern part of the city, linked to downtown by the Truman Parkway.
  • Eastside and Westside: two more of the city's principal areas.
  • Southwest and West Chatham: suburban areas annexed more recently.

Besides the main Savannah Historic District, five other districts are formally marked: Victorian, Cuyler-Brownville, Thomas Square, Pin Point, and Ardsley Park-Chatham Crescent. If your house lies inside a district, phone the city's planning staff about review of exterior changes such as windows, siding or porches before you start work.

Flood risk is the practical issue. Savannah is prone to flooding because of heavy rainfall, an elevation just above sea level and the shape of the coastline, and the city uses five canals and several pumping stations to manage flash flooding. Hurricanes have affected the area, among them Matthew in 2016, Irma in 2017, and Debby and Helene in 2024. Expect buyers to ask about water in the yard, crawl spaces and prior claims.

Gather what you have before listing: repair receipts, drainage work, any flood insurance paperwork, and photos from past storms. If the house has unrepaired storm damage, an as-is sale may fit better than a listing that requires a buyer's lender to approve the condition.

sections.h2: Can a former Savannah vacation rental be sold?
sections.html:
You can sell it, but Savannah regulates these rentals tightly. The city defines a short-term vacation rental as lodging in a residential unit for no more than 30 consecutive days, and renting a single room is regulated separately as a bed and breakfast homestay. Where rentals are allowed depends on location:

  • Inside the overlay district, which covers the Downtown, Victorian and Streetcar local historic districts.
  • Outside the overlay, only in the B-C, B-N, B-L and A-1 zoning classes.
  • In the Downtown and Victorian districts, new rentals in residential areas are capped at 20 percent of residential parcels in each ward, with owner-occupied parcels exempt.
  • Applications filed before September 28, 2017 were grandfathered and may be renewed.

The city's fees are $400 for a new application and $250 for annual renewal, both non-refundable, and applications go through the city's STVR registration portal. A buyer who plans to keep renting the house should contact the city office listed on the STVR page before closing to learn what the buyer must file.

sections.h2: City of Savannah property tax bills and late charges
sections.html:
The City of Savannah collects its own property tax in two installments, apart from the county and school bills. The city's Revenue Department sends the first bill in April, typically due in mid-June and based on half of the prior year's tax. The second goes out in September, typically due in mid-November, and reflects that year's value, exemptions and millage. Due dates are set when the bills are printed, so check the bill itself.

Only 40 percent of the appraised figure is taxable under state law, the appraisal comes from the Chatham County assessors, and anyone living in the city pays county tax and city tax. School board taxes are collected by the Chatham County Tax Commissioner. The city does not offer payment plans, and a payment is on time only if it posts to the account by the due date.

Billing step or penaltyRule
First installmentBilled in April, typically due mid-June, based on half of prior year
Second installmentBilled in September, typically due mid-November
Interest on delinquent taxPrime rate plus 3 percent annually, accruing monthly
Penalty5 percent once 120 days late, repeating every 120 days up to 20 percent
Bill under appealBilled at prior year value or 85 percent of current value, whichever is less

The Revenue Department's property tax unit, 912-651-6455, can supply a copy of any bill you did not receive, since a lost bill is no defense to a late fee.

sections.h2: Homestead exemption, appeals and tax sales
sections.html:
Homestead exemption applications go to the Chatham County Board of Assessors at 222 West Oglethorpe Avenue, Suite 113, and the phone number is 912-652-7271. To qualify, you must have owned the home and lived there as your permanent residence on January 1. Rentals are excluded. Filing by the 45-day appeal date on your annual notice covers the current year, and filing later covers the next.

An appeal must answer an annual assessment notice, and the window runs 45 days from the date it shows. The assessors measure square footage on file from the exterior perimeter, which often differs from the living area an owner measures inside, so check that before you argue.

If taxes stay unpaid, the city holds about six tax sales each year. An owner may redeem within a year and a day by paying the winning bidder the bid plus 20 percent. A seller who has fallen behind should clear delinquent tax and any Fi. Fa. lien before closing, since the lien must be satisfied for a clean title to pass.

sections.h2: Which routes sell a Savannah house fastest?
sections.html:
Owners here usually weigh three routes: an agent listing, an as-is investor sale, or a direct cash sale. A public listing can fetch the best price for a clean, updated house, though it brings open houses, inspections and a financing risk.

Selling for cash gives up some price in return for a firm closing date, which can suit houses with deferred repairs, tenants, probate or tax problems. Whatever route you choose, ask for the net figure after taxes, liens and closing costs, and verify every payoff before you sign.

Georgia's transfer tax also applies to the deed. Ask your closing attorney who pays it under your contract, and request a draft settlement statement early so you can check the tax line, the payoff and any lien release before closing day.

faqs.q: When do Savannah city taxes come due?
faqs.a: The city's two installments are typically due in mid-June and mid-November. The exact dates are set when the bills are printed, so read your bill.

faqs.q: Can I still apply for homestead exemption if I miss April 1?
faqs.a: Yes, if you file by the 45-day appeal due date on your notice of assessment, the Board of Assessors considers it for the current year. Later applications apply to the following year.

faqs.q: Could my Savannah house be a vacation rental?
faqs.a: Only if it sits in the overlay district or one of the B-C, B-N, B-L or A-1 zones, and downtown residential areas face a 20 percent ward cap. Owner-occupied parcels are exempt from the cap.

faqs.q: What happens if I lose my house at a Savannah tax sale?
faqs.a: You can redeem within a year and a day by paying the winning bidder the bid amount plus 20 percent. Contact the bidder directly to arrange it.

faqs.q: Who decides what my Savannah home is worth for tax?
faqs.a: The Chatham County Board of Assessors does, and the city levies its own tax on that value. Appeals start with the notice of assessment and a 45-day window.
